thread.title: Can Fitbit Be Worth $15 By The End Of The Year? - Fitbit, Inc. (NYSE:FIT)

author: Daniel Schönberger
title: Can Fitbit Be Worth $15 By The End Of The Year? - Fitbit, Inc. (NYSE:FIT)
text:
"Citron has done the analysis that NO ONE on Wall Street has taken the time to fully analyze and appreciate. Based on our work and the information that follows, we will explain why $FIT steps all the way up to $15/share in 2018 if not acquired first."
With this bold statement , Citron Research was quite able to move the market, and by claiming the stock has about 140% upside and will reach $15 within 6 months, the stock rallied almost 20% that day. On the same day, Fitbit (NYSE: FIT ) also reported its Fitbit Ace wearable will be globally available for kids ages 8 and up, and at that point in time, shares were already up 4-5% that day.
The obvious question right now is: Can Fitbit really be worth $15 within the next 6 months? Or was it all - like some people claim - only a "pump-and-dump" action? The following article will be divided into two major sections to provide an answer to that question. In the first part, we will mostly look at the numbers, the stock and its valuation (as well as sentiment), and in the second part of the article, we will look at the fundamental side of the business and examine how the company could grow again and develop in the future.
I. Stock And Sentiment A few years ago, Fitbit was profitable and reported earnings per share of $0.81 for 2014 and $0.88 for 2015, while right now the company had to report a net loss for two years in a row. To make matters worse, revenue was also higher in 2015 and 2016. And right now, the combination of declining revenue and a loss per share led to a terrible sentiment, which was surrounding Fitbit the last two years.
But not all numbers are negative. When looking at the balance sheet, I think we can be quite impressed. Aside from $54 million in "other long-term liabilities," the company doesn't have any short- or long-term debt - a rarity for young companies. Fitbit also has $658 million in cash and cash equivalents, and the shareholders' equity is $762 million. Compared to the current market cap of about $1.74 billion, we get a price book value ratio of 2.35 (rather low for a tech company). Therefore, we have a company that couldn't manage to stay profitable and suffered from declining revenue but presents itself as very healthy one with almost no obligations or debt and a big pile of money it can use for acquisitions or further research.
Intrinsic Value Calculation
When looking at the chart and the different price levels of the stock during its rather short life, the conclusion must be that it is rather hard to value Fitbit, and different investors obviously have very different opinions about the fair value of the stock. After its IPO, the stock rallied to over $50 and then declined more than 90% to under $5 - extreme price swings. And again, in the last two weeks, the stock rallied almost 40%. These extreme price swings show us that there is obviously no consensus among different market participants what the stock should be worth and hence it is jumping widely. One simple explanation is the hype cycle every new company (or invention) passes through. I already mentioned this in my first article about Fitbit. Times of inflated expectations are followed by the trough of disillusionment, and the stock price development feels like a roller-coaster ride.
Another reason for these extreme price swings is the difficulty to decide what a realistic growth rate for the company's revenue and net income should be. The one extreme would be those who think Fitbit will have to file bankruptcy within a few years and value it accordingly - with an intrinsic value next to nothing. The other extreme is unrealistic expectations about astronomic growth rates - probably an accurate description of the sentiment right after the IPO. Our job right now is to provide a reasonable assessment about the future development of Fitbit.
I will also not claim that I know how to value Fitbit, and I also have troubles to calculate an exact intrinsic value as there are many unknown factors. In the following second part of the article, we will discuss a few different perspectives and arguments to guide the reader on the path to a realistic intrinsic value calculation for Fitbit.
II. The Fundamental Business A first important point that is worth mentioning is the high number of devices sold of Fitbit's new smartwatch Versa . In about seven weeks between the mid April and the beginning of June, Fitbit sold over 1 million devices . This alone will lead to a revenue of $200 million. Even if we can assume that sales probably will slow down in the following weeks, it might sell close to 1.5 million devices, and of course, this is not the only device Fitbit is selling. Hence, I think we can assume revenue to increase quite a bit YoY for the second quarter of 2018.
Smartwatch as medical device?
As the name suggests, Fitbit's main focus is on fitness, and it seems quite natural to expand into areas that are closely attached to fitness - like personal wellbeing. The smartwatch Versa with its different functions can still be seen as fitness device. Fitbit however is trying to move into the highly profitable medical segment. Different partnerships with insurance companies and the partnership with Medtronic (NYSE: MDT ) are underlining this development. Already in December 2016, Fitbit and Medtronic introduced the Pro 2 myLog mobile app, which allows patients to see their glucose levels as well as their physical activity data in one streamlined application. That was a first hint in which direction Fitbit will develop - a tech company that is combining fitness and healthcare data.
In this context, we have to mention the amount of money Fitbit is spending on research and development . Citron Research is pointing out in its report that Fitbit spent over $700 million on research and development since 2016. In the last four quarters, the company spent 22% of its revenue on research and development, and in the last quarter alone, 36% of revenue was spent on R&D.
New functions
If we assume that Fitbit will transform into a medical device company, we have to ask ourselves where the benefit for the company is and how a smartwatch or fitness tracker can become a device for medical purposes. The McKinsey study, " The Internet of Things: Mapping the value beyond the hype ," can be a valuable source of information to answer that question. The study focuses - among other topics - on the healthcare sector. Wearables could not just be used for real-time treatment management, but also for early detection of complications. And to be more specific, wearables that could measure weight, exercise, heart rate, body temperature and blood pressure could be used for early detection and treatment of heart diseases, HIV/AIDS and diabetes for example. McKinsey estimates the market size somewhere between $170 billion on the low end and $1,590 billion on the upper end for devices that are attached to or are inside the human body (see p. 37-49).
Especially diabetes is a serious disease affecting millions of people around the globe and a good example how fitness tracker and smartwatches can be used for medical purposes. The number of diabetics right now is over 400 million worldwide, and the number will grow from year to year to about 650 million in 2040 - a gigantic market. At this point, it is important to understand the two (main) types of diabetes - type-1 diabetes and type-2 diabetes. Whereas type-1 diabetes can't be cured so far and patients have to live with the disease their whole lives, type-2 diabetes is massively affected by obesity and the fitness level of a person. And out of the 30 million diabetics in the United States, about 95% are type-2 diabetics (latest estimates expect 29 million). It certainly would be unfair (and not true at all) that every type-2 diabetic suffers from the disease because of too less exercise. But it is also a fact that a lot of type-2 diabetics would need less insulin or other medication, if they lived healthier and lost weight. For type-2 diabetics, regular exercise could have a positive effect on the glucose levels and reduce the need for insulin. If millions of diabetics would start using a fitness tracker to monitor their regular exercises, this could be a massive boost for Fitbit's revenue.
Who should pay?
A valid objection at this point is the question why the millions of diabetics should buy a fitness tracker in the future, when they didn't do so in the past. We can present two counter-arguments and think about two potential developments to "solve that problem":
Third-party payers Smartwatches being accepted as medical devices If third-party payers are covering the costs, the number of devices sold could increase massively. There are two types of organizations that could serve as third-party payer - employers who buy wearables for the employees and health insurance companies that cover the costs and interested in healthier insured persons. Fitbit is presenting its " Group Health Program " on its homepage and some companies that already work with it. It is rather obvious why companies and corporations should be interested in healthy employees - they will be far less ill and will stay healthier even in the years before retirement. This leads to a reduced loss of working hours and reduces overall costs for the company. A second opportunity would be health insurance companies that cover the costs in similar ways as other treatments or medical devices (like insulin pumps or CGM systems) are covered. As long as individuals have to pay for a fitness tracker, the number of people purchasing it may be rather low. But when the same people only have to pay indirect for the costs, they probably won't care. Raise the monthly insurance fee a few dollars and insurance companies can pay for fitness tracker.
Aside from a third-party payer, the second big opportunity is the transformation of fitness devices in medical devices with additional features. In order to treat diabetes for example, Fitbit's smartwatch has to become a continuous glucose monitoring system - like those devices DexCom (NASDAQ: DXCM ) or Abbott Laboratories (NYSE: ABT ) offer. Fitbit would go down a similar road as Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) is (presumably) going down right now. Last year there were different information that the tech giant will focus its research and development on how to enter the healthcare market and making the Apple watch a medical device. In May 2017 it was reported that Apple is working on its own, non-invasive version of a CGM system connected to the Apple watch. If a Fitbit smartwatch can not only just be a fitness device but also monitor blood sugar levels, display current data and also control the insulin pump, companies like Apple or Fitbit could become a major threat for DexCom or the diabetes segment of Abbott Laboratories and Medtronic.
In the sections above we mostly focused on diabetes, but of course, there are other diseases worth mentioning because wearables could play an important role in early detection of complications and real-time treatment management. In the following chart of McKinsey we see a good overview:

Smartwatch as data collector?
Aside from partnerships with DexCom or Medtronic, Fitbit also announced a partnership with Google (NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ) in April 2018. Both companies will work together and explore the development of consumer and enterprise health solutions. The two companies will help to better manage chronic conditions like diabetes and hypertension by using services like Fitbit's recently acquired Twine Health. And aside from generating revenue by selling hardware, we also have to focus on different ways to monetize the massive amount of data Fitbit is collecting. With a network of 25 million active users, the amount of collected data is quite impressive.
(Source: SunTrust Robinson Humphrey Internet & Digital Media Conference )
Jason Park already realized last year that especially the data Fitbit is collecting about sleep is extremely important and could be valuable:
"Traditionally measured in an expensive sleep lab, consumers can now use our tracker to estimate their respective sleep stages in a more convenient and comfortable way. Sleep is one of the most engaged sections of the app. Fitbit users have logged more than 3 billion nights of sleep. To put this into context, that's equivalent to about 2.5 million years." (Earnings Call Q1/17)
The comparison may be a bit farfetched, but Fitbit is somewhat in the same situation as Google was about one and a half decades earlier. Just as Google, Fitbit is collecting big amounts of data every day and it has to figure out how it could monetize the collected data. This could be a way for Fitbit to not just sell devices and generate its revenue through wristbands and smartwatches but also from the collected data. Depending on which fitness tracker a person uses, Fitbit has data about the steps and the distance a person walks every day as well as the number of floors. Additionally, it has the heart rate for these persons 24/7 and data about the sleep of millions of users. Depending on what users record in the app, it also has information about the eating and drinking habits as well as the weight every single day. It will be on Fitbit's management team to figure out how these massive amounts of data can be monetized.
Conclusion The provoking headline was if Fitbit could reach $15 per share at the end of the year - like Citron Research claims. The answer to this question mostly depends on sentiment . If we compare a few companies, I think this point becomes very clear. In the following chart, we see three valuation metrics for four different companies.
(Source: Own Work)
These numbers clearly show how undervalued Fitbit is (or how overvalued the other three companies are). While Fitbit is worth about the same amount it can generate as annual revenue, DexCom and Netflix (NASDAQ: NFLX ) are valued 11 times or even 13 times the annual generated revenue. Price to book value is usually higher for tech companies as these companies often don't have much tangible assets, but the differences between Fitbit and Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN ) or Netflix are speaking volumes. In the end, the explanation is very simple: For DexCom, Amazon or Netflix, the current valuation is based on (doubtful) expectations of extreme (never-ending) growth, while Fitbit is the classic example of a company where investors are expecting the worst.
So, we ask again: Can Fitbit be worth $15 per share in December 2018? If sentiment changes and Fitbit will be valued like DexCom or Netflix, we will not only reach $15 per share but might also see much higher numbers. Just for fun: Citron Research is providing a comparison at the end of its analysis and comes to the conclusion that Fitbit could be worth $71 per share (Citron itself calls this unrealistic, but with the same sentiment surrounding Amazon and Netflix, this would probably be the current price for Fitbit on the stock exchange).
But we don't want a stock price that is solely based on extreme sentiment swings, but is reflective of the real value of a company. And although I have my doubts if Fitbit can reach $15 per share in 2018, I think the stock is undervalued. I am quite aware that the all the mentioned points are arguable and doubtful and also rather uncertain. Therefore, it would be idiotic to dream that Fitbit will become the next Apple or the next Google, but the company has definitely the potential to become an important player in its market.
Disclosure: I am/we are long FIT.
